# What is the self assessment tax return deadline? Key dates explained

:::answer
The self assessment tax return deadline is the date HMRC sets for submitting your online return and paying any tax due, which falls on 31 January following the end of the tax year. Miss it and you face an automatic penalty plus interest on anything unpaid.
:::

:::takeaways
- The online self assessment deadline is 31 January after the tax year ends.
- Not everyone is sent a return automatically, so you must check whether you need to submit one.
- Late filing brings an automatic penalty, and interest builds on any unpaid tax.
- Leaving a return to the last weeks increases the risk of errors and fraud attempts.
- Accountants often stop taking on new self assessment clients from October, so early contact matters.
:::

## What is the self assessment tax return deadline?

The self assessment tax return deadline is the final date HMRC allows for filing your return and settling the tax you owe for a given tax year. For most people filing online, this falls on 31 January following the end of the tax year in question. [Alexander & Co](https://alexander.co.uk/news/31-january-self-assessment-deadline-is-approaching/) notes that this is often framed as approaching fast once autumn arrives, since the gap between the October half-term and January is shorter than it looks.

Not everyone has to complete a return. Some people, those who are self-employed, for example, need to complete a tax return every year, while others are only sent one because they have untaxed income, often from property, as [Alexander & Co](https://alexander.co.uk/news/31-january-self-assessment-deadline-is-approaching/) explains. HMRC does not always know your full employment status, so the responsibility to check sits with you, not with the taxman.

## How does the self assessment deadline work?

The deadline works on a cycle tied to the tax year, which runs to 5 April. Once that year closes, HMRC expects your online return and payment by the following 31 January, giving you roughly ten months to gather records, calculate income, and submit.

In practice, the window feels shorter than the calendar suggests. As one Alexander & Co update put it, as of today, 23 October, there is just 100 days to go, and when you factor in the Christmas break, this means even less time. That squeeze is why many people leave it until the last minute, or even past the deadline, to submit their return, according to [Alexander & Co](https://alexander.co.uk/news/31-january-self-assessment-deadline-is-approaching/). Filing early does not change the deadline itself, but it changes how much pressure you are under when it arrives, and how much time an adviser has to check your figures before submission.

## What are the filing options and their limits?

Self assessment offers a small number of routes, each with its own cut-off and consequence if missed. The table below sets out the main ones.

| Filing route | Deadline | Consequence of missing it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Online tax return and payment | 31 January after the tax year ends | Automatic penalty and interest charges apply |
| Paper tax return | Earlier than the online deadline | Late paper filing also attracts penalty fines |
| Registering for self assessment for the first time | Before you can file, well ahead of 31 January | Delays registration and risks missing the filing deadline itself |

The limit that catches people out is time with an accountant, not just time with HMRC. Many accountants stop taking on new clients from October, and may even struggle to act for existing clients who have not sent information early, as [Alexander & Co](https://alexander.co.uk/news/31-january-self-assessment-deadline-is-approaching/) states. Anyone in either position is advised to make contact as early as possible.

## What does a missed deadline look like in practice?

Consider the rule HMRC applied for the 2018-2019 tax year: if HMRC has asked you to complete a self assessment return for 2018-2019, you must complete it before 31 January 2020 or face a fine, as recorded by [Alexander & Co](https://alexander.co.uk/news/31-january-self-assessment-deadline-is-approaching/). That single sentence captures the whole mechanism, a named tax year, a fixed date the following January, and a penalty attached to missing it.

The same pattern repeats every year, only the dates shift forward by twelve months. Someone filing for the most recent tax year faces the same structure, the same late-filing penalty, and the same interest charge on any tax paid after the date, just applied to a different year's figures.

## What happens if you miss the self assessment deadline?

Missing the deadline triggers an automatic penalty from HMRC, and interest then accrues on any tax that remains unpaid. [Alexander & Co](https://alexander.co.uk/news/31-january-self-assessment-deadline-is-approaching/) states plainly that late filing can attract penalty fines and interest charges, and the longer a return stays outstanding, the more both can add up.

There is a second, less obvious cost. Rushing a return in the final days makes you more susceptible to mistakes, and it also leaves you more exposed to reported fraud attacks that target people scrambling to file at the last moment, according to [Alexander & Co](https://alexander.co.uk/news/31-january-self-assessment-deadline-is-approaching/). Filing earlier removes both risks at once.
